title: Poor balance? Read this story.
body:
I spent 40 years as an orthopedic surgeon. I repaired over 3,000 broken hips with my own two hands. And I'm about to tell you something I should have said 20 years ago.
My family told me to let it go. I'm retired now. Nobody's career is on the line anymore — not mine, not the podiatrists', not the hospital's. But I'm 71 years old, and I set too many broken bones back into place knowing the truth and saying nothing.
So here it is.
When you operate on a broken hip, you don't just see the fracture. You handle what's around it. You feel the difference between a leg that was strong and a leg that had been wasting from the inside while its owner was still walking around, still going to the store, still telling her daughter her checkup came back fine.
And in 40 years, in patient after patient that came across my table, I found the same thing.

body:
You lose the feeling in your toes before you ever sit down. You just don't know it yet.

The walk in generates heat. Your feet sweat inside the boots. Normal. You don't notice because you're moving, you're warm, everything feels fine.

Then you reach the stand. Settle in. Stop moving.

Fifteen minutes later, your toes start going cold. Thirty minutes, they're stiff. An hour in, you can barely feel them. 

Toe warmers buy you maybe another 45 minutes before those fade too. 

And now you're watching the clock instead of the timber.

The cold didn't freeze your toes. The moisture from the walk in did. 

It's been sitting against your skin this whole time, and the second your body stopped producing heat, it started pulling warmth out of your feet faster than your body can replace it.

Thicker socks make this worse. More bulk means less room in the toe box. 

Less room means less circulation and less of that dead-air pocket that actually insulates your toes.

title: 14+ Hours. No Swelling. No Painful Red Marks.
body:
If you hate your compression socks, they may just be the wrong material

Nobody shops for compression socks by fiber. You look at the compression level, maybe the height, maybe the price.

The material? It's an afterthought. Usually cotton. Sometimes a polyester blend. Whatever's in there, you don't think about it.

Until you're four hours into wearing them and your feet are damp, hot, and starting to smell... and you realize the compression is fine but you can't stand the sock anymore.

That's a fiber problem. And it's the reason a lot of people buy compression socks, wear them for a week, and quietly stop.

Cotton absorbs moisture. In a regular sock, that's annoying. In a compression sock where everything is tighter and there's less airflow, it turns your foot into a sweat trap. 

The moisture has nowhere to go. It just sits there getting warmer and heavier until you give up and take them off mid-afternoon.

Hollow makes their compression socks from alpaca. Different animal entirely.

title: Alpaca Hunt Socks
body:
You lose the feeling in your toes before you ever sit down. You just don't know it yet.

The walk in generates heat. Your feet sweat inside the boots. Normal. You don't notice because you're moving, you're warm, everything feels fine.

Then you reach the stand. Settle in. Stop moving.

Fifteen minutes later, your toes start going cold. Thirty minutes, they're stiff. An hour in, you can barely feel them. 

Toe warmers buy you maybe another 45 minutes before those fade too. 

And now you're watching the clock instead of the timber.

The cold didn't freeze your toes. The moisture from the walk in did. 

It's been sitting against your skin this whole time, and the second your body stopped producing heat, it started pulling warmth out of your feet faster than your body can replace it.

Thicker socks make this worse. More bulk means less room in the toe box. 

Less room means less circulation and less of that dead-air pocket that actually insulates your toes. 

Plus heavy wool absorbs sweat
